newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Security tops priorities for new Kuwait cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Security tops priorities for new Kuwait cabinet.

text.p: Kuwait swore in a new government on Wednesday that will give top priority to strengthening defences against former occupier Iraq.

"National security...has been and will always be our main duty and a sacred task that takes priority over any other issue," Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah told his new government.
He said in a televised speech that the tiny oil state's entire resources should be devoted to safeguarding internal and external security.
The 14-man cabinet formed on Tuesday night includes new ministers for oil, interior and defence.
Defence Minister Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah, 59, will oversee a $11.7 billion plan covering the years 1992 to 2004 to rebuild the military after the 1990 Iraqi invasion.
He will also stay in close contact with Washington and other Western allies who led the 1991 Gulf War against Iraq to ensure their continued commitment to Kuwait's defence.
Last month the United States sent troops and eight stealth bombers to Kuwait in the face of what officials called renewed Iraqi threats.
Sheikh Saad told the first cabinet meeting that the government "will continue building the security, national defence, national unity and an effective economy".
Other key priorities listed by Sheikh Saad, prime minister since 1978, included "completing economic reforms, eliminating the state budget deficit and boosting general administration and services".
The cabinet, which includes four elected MPs, was formed after last week's parliamentary elections dominated by debates about Iraqi threats.
The parliament, which starts its four-year term on Sunday, is seen as less confrontational than the last opposition- dominated one. Many pro-government MPs won seats.

Kuwait's first parliament after the Gulf War investigated alleged official corruption and misuse of public funds. It also questioned arms deals with Western allies and the state's handling of events before Iraq's occupation.
It passed a $14 billion budget for fiscal 1996/97 with a forecast $4 billion deficit. Kuwait has said it plans to balance the budget by 2000 after huge losses during the Gulf crisis.
The opposition weekly al-Talea on Wednesday attacked the new government, saying Kuwait was heading towards "another period of immobility and muddling".
"The malfunction will remain unchanged or it will even worsen," said the mouthpiece of the left-leaning Kuwait Democratic Forum, which groups liberal, pan-Arab nationalists.
Besides Sheikh Saad, 66, the cabinet has four other members of the al-Sabah family that has ruled since 1752.
"It has become unbearable for the country that members of the ruling family continue to hold the sovereignty ministries in addition to the premier's post," added al-Talea.
The ministers of information, interior and foreign affairs are all members of the ruling family.
